conversation.content: Let's design a real-time chat system like WhatsApp or Slack. It should support one-on-one and group messaging. What questions do you have?
Key questions: What's the expected number of concurrent connections? What's the message delivery latency target? Do we need message persistence and history? And what's the maximum group size?
10 million concurrent WebSocket connections at peak. Message delivery under 100ms. Yes to persistence — full message history. Groups up to 500 members. Go ahead.

The thing that immediately jumps out to me is: how do we deploy a new version of the WebSocket gateway without dropping 10 million connections? That's my biggest operational concern, and I want to design for it from the start. Let me lay out the architecture with deployability as a first-class concern.
That's an important concern. Walk me through the architecture.

I'll separate the system into layers that can be deployed independently. Layer 1: WebSocket Gateway — maintains persistent connections, handles protocol (connect, disconnect, heartbeat). Stateful but dumb — it just routes messages. Layer 2: Chat Service — stateless business logic: send message, create group, fetch history. Layer 3: Presence Service — tracks who's online, last seen. Layer 4: Message Store — Cassandra for message persistence. Layer 5: Notification Service — push notifications for offline users. The key insight is that the gateway is the hardest to deploy because it holds state (connections), so I want to minimize what lives there and make it independently deployable from the business logic.
Good separation. Now, how do you deploy a new version of the gateway without dropping those 10M connections?

Blue-green deployment with connection draining. Here's the process: We have two pools of gateway servers — blue (current, serving traffic) and green (new version, idle). Step 1: Deploy the new version to the green pool. Run smoke tests against green — verify WebSocket handshake, message routing, heartbeat. Step 2: Update the load balancer to send all NEW connections to green. Existing connections on blue continue working. Step 3: Connection draining on blue. The blue servers stop accepting new connections and send a 'reconnect' control message to connected clients. The client SDK handles this gracefully — it disconnects and immediately reconnects, hitting the green pool. We drain gradually: 10% of connections per minute over 10 minutes. Step 4: Once blue has zero connections, decommission it. The total rollout takes about 15 minutes. Users experience a brief reconnection — invisible if the client SDK handles it properly.
What if something goes wrong with the green deployment? How do you roll back?

Rollback has three scenarios. Scenario 1: Issue caught during smoke tests on green, before any traffic shift. Easy — just don't proceed. Green stays idle, blue keeps serving. Scenario 2: Issue detected during the draining phase (maybe green's error rate spikes). We stop the drain immediately, flip the load balancer back so new connections go to blue, and send reconnect signals from green back to blue. We've only migrated a fraction of users so the blast radius is small. Scenario 3: Issue detected after full migration to green. This is the worst case — we need to treat blue as the new target and drain green back to blue. This is why I keep the old blue deployment warm and ready for at least 1 hour after migration. The monitoring that triggers rollback: if green's connection drop rate exceeds 5% or message delivery failure rate exceeds 0.1%, automatic rollback initiates.
How does the client SDK handle the reconnection transparently?

The client SDK implements a reconnection protocol. When it receives the server's 'reconnect' control frame, it: 1) Stores the last received message sequence number locally. 2) Closes the current WebSocket cleanly. 3) Reconnects to the gateway (which the LB routes to the green pool). 4) Sends a 'resume' frame with user_id and last_sequence_number. 5) The new gateway server fetches any messages the client missed (from the message store) and delivers them. The client shows no visible disruption — it might see a brief spinner at most. The SDK also has exponential backoff with jitter for reconnection in case the green pool is temporarily overwhelmed. We buffer outbound messages locally during reconnection and flush them once connected. The protocol version is negotiated during handshake, so old clients talking to new servers still work via backward compatibility.
Interesting. Let's discuss how you deploy the Chat Service — the stateless layer.

The Chat Service is much easier since it's stateless. I'd use rolling deployments in Kubernetes. With 50 replicas, we update 5 at a time (maxSurge: 5, maxUnavailable: 5). Each new pod runs readiness probes — health check endpoint that verifies database connectivity, Redis connectivity, and Kafka producer health. Only when ready does it receive traffic. I'd add a pre-stop hook that waits 15 seconds before shutdown, giving in-flight requests time to complete. For database schema changes that accompany a Chat Service deploy, I use the expand-and-contract pattern: first deploy code that writes to both old and new schema, then migrate data, then deploy code that only uses new schema, then drop old columns. This ensures zero downtime for schema changes too.
How do you handle deploying changes that affect the message format or protocol?

Protocol versioning with forward and backward compatibility. Every WebSocket message has a version field. The gateway and chat service support the current version N and the previous version N-1 simultaneously. When we deploy a new message format, it's version N+1 alongside N. Deployment sequence: 1) Deploy gateway that understands both N and N+1 but still sends N. 2) Deploy chat service that handles both versions. 3) Deploy gateway that starts sending N+1 to clients that negotiate it. 4) After 2 release cycles, drop support for N-1. I use Protocol Buffers for message serialization — they handle field addition/removal gracefully. Unknown fields are preserved, not dropped. This means even if the gateway and chat service are temporarily on different versions during deployment, messages pass through correctly.
Let's talk about the data layer. How do you deploy Cassandra schema changes without downtime?

Cassandra is relatively deployment-friendly because ALTER TABLE ADD column is non-blocking and doesn't lock. For adding a column: add it to Cassandra, deploy application code that writes to it, backfill historical data with a Spark job, then start reading from it. For removing a column: deploy code that stops reading, deploy code that stops writing, then drop the column. The dangerous operation is changing a partition key or clustering column — that requires creating a new table, dual-writing, migrating data, and switching reads. I'd do this as a multi-phase deployment over several days, not a single release. For Cassandra node upgrades (e.g., version 3.x to 4.x), I'd do rolling upgrades: decommission one node at a time, let data stream to replicas, upgrade, rejoin. With replication factor 3, we always maintain quorum.
How do you test a deployment before it reaches production?

Four environments in the pipeline. Dev — runs integration tests with in-memory dependencies. Staging — full topology mirror of production at 1/10th scale. This is where we run the deployment procedure itself — blue-green for gateway, rolling for chat service — to verify the mechanics. Load test environment — staging topology but with synthetic traffic generators pushing 10M simulated connections to verify the connection draining works at scale. We simulate all the failure modes: what if a client doesn't respond to the reconnect signal? What if the green pool isn't ready when connections arrive? Canary in production — deploy to 2% of traffic first. Monitor for 30 minutes. If connection error rate, message delivery latency, and crash rate are all within 5% of baseline, proceed with full rollout.
What about feature flags? How do they fit into this?

Feature flags are essential for decoupling deployment from release. I'd use a feature flag service like LaunchDarkly or a self-hosted system backed by etcd. New features ship behind flags — the code is deployed to all servers, but the feature is only enabled for internal users initially, then 1% of users, then 10%, then 100%. This means deployment is routine and boring — we deploy daily or even multiple times a day. Risky features get their own kill switch. If a new message threading feature causes performance issues, I flip the flag off in seconds without a deployment. The gateway's reconnection protocol can also be flagged — if the new graceful reconnection logic has a bug, we fall back to the old hard-disconnect behavior. Flags have TTLs: if a flag has been 100% on for 30 days, a bot creates a PR to remove it from code to prevent flag debt.
Let's talk about capacity planning for deployments. During a blue-green switch, you're running double the gateway servers.

Right, that's a real cost. During the 15-minute deployment window, we need 2x the gateway capacity. At 10M connections, with each server handling about 100K connections, that's 100 servers normally and 200 during deployment. The cost mitigation: we schedule deployments during low-traffic windows — say 2am UTC when we have 4M connections, not 10M. That means we only need 40 + 40 = 80 servers instead of 200. Alternatively, we could use a canary approach instead of full blue-green: deploy to 5 servers, drain them, verify, then roll through the fleet in batches of 10. This never requires more than 10 extra servers but takes longer — about 1 hour for the full fleet. The trade-off is deployment speed versus infrastructure cost. I'd use the canary approach for routine releases and full blue-green only for critical patches that need fast rollout.
How do you handle the case where a deploy introduces a subtle message ordering bug that only manifests under load?

This is the hardest class of bugs to catch. My defense layers: First, the message sequence numbers I mentioned earlier. Every message in a conversation has a monotonically increasing sequence number. The client SDK can detect out-of-order delivery and report it as a metric. If the out-of-order rate exceeds 0.01% after a deploy, alert and investigate. Second, a shadow validation system: in staging, we run a deterministic message replay — we record a day of production message patterns (anonymized) and replay them through the new version. We compare output ordering against the known-correct baseline. Third, in production, a real-time audit trail: every message routing decision is logged with timestamps. When an ordering bug is reported, we can reconstruct exactly what happened. The mitigation: if an ordering bug is confirmed, feature-flag the change off immediately, don't wait for a full rollback.
We're almost out of time. Summarize your deployment philosophy.

Three principles. First, make deployments boring — deploy frequently with small changes so each deployment is low risk. Feature flags decouple deployment from release. Second, design for rollback from the start — every deployment artifact, every schema change, every protocol version must be reversible. The question isn't if we'll need to roll back, it's when. Third, stateful components (WebSocket gateway, database) need special deployment strategies (blue-green with draining, rolling with compatibility), while stateless components are straightforward. The architecture should minimize statefulness to minimize deployment complexity.
Strong interview. Excellent operational thinking. Thank you.

strengths: Exceptional deployment strategy for stateful WebSocket connections with detailed blue-green and draining approach
Strong operational thinking — rollback, feature flags, protocol versioning all well-covered
Good understanding of the cost and risk trade-offs of different deployment approaches
weaknesses: Caching strategy was not discussed at all
Message delivery guarantees and consistency model were underexplored
Didn't discuss multi-region deployment or geo-routing
